0.value:
Overwrites chosen positions in an array with a value you type.

Name the positions in "indices", put the new value in "values", and every array that passes through comes out with those positions replaced. It is for patching a few numbers by hand: zeroing a channel you do not trust, pinning a calibration value, forcing one element of a weight vector while you tune.

IT DOES NOT DISPLAY THE ARRAY:
np.edit shows only the two fields. Put a display after it - a heat_map, as here, for a grid - to see the result.

WRITING INDICES:
The same slice notation as numpy, one entry per dimension, separated by commas:

  2        just position 2
  1:3      positions 1 and 2 (the end is not included)
  3:       from position 3 to the end
  :        everything
  0, 1:3   in row 0, columns 1 and 2

Dimensions you leave out are taken whole, so on a grid "2" means all of row 2. -1 means the last position.

NOTHING HAPPENS UNTIL YOU TYPE A VALUE:
A fresh np.edit has indices ":" and an empty "values" field, and passes arrays through unchanged until you put something in "values". Clearing the field again turns the edit off.

WHAT THE VALUE CAN BE:
A single number fills every chosen position. A list of numbers fills them in order: "1 2" into "3:5" puts 1 at position 3 and 2 at position 4. A list longer than the selection is cut short. For a grid, a list as long as a row is copied into every chosen row; a list of any other length is ignored on a grid (nothing changes, without a message).

The value takes the array's own type, so 2.7 written into an integer array becomes 2.

EDITS WITHOUT A NEW ARRAY:
Changing either field re-sends straight away, applied to a fresh copy of the last array that arrived - so only the current edit shows (set 1:3 to 9, then change indices to 4, and only position 4 is 9).

SYNTAX:
np.edit <indices>

EXAMPLE:
np.edit 1:3, 2:6

INPUTS and PARAMETERS:

array in:
The array. Receiving it triggers the node.

indices:
Which positions to replace.

values:
What to put there.

widget width (option):
How wide to draw the two fields. They can also be dragged wider.

OUTPUTS:

output:
A copy of the array with the edit applied. The incoming array itself is not changed.

READING THE DEMO:
np.rand makes a 5 x 8 grid of numbers between 0 and 0.5 - all dark - and the left heat_map shows it. np.edit writes 1 into rows 1 and 2, columns 2 to 5, and the right heat_map shows the result: the same grid with a bright block in it. Every other cell is untouched.

Type into the fields and the right picture changes at once: indices "0" for all of row 0, ":, 7" for the last column, "4, 0" for one cell; values "0.25" for a middle shade, or a whole row of eight such as "0 1 0 1 0 1 0 1" to stripe the chosen rows. Click np.rand for a fresh grid - the same edit is applied to it.

RELATED:
np.[] reads positions out instead of writing them. np.where replaces values by a condition rather than by position. np.clip limits values; np.zeros and np.ones make an array to edit into.
